titleStmt.title: Lessons from the use of non-invasive genetic sampling as a way to estimate Eurasian otter population size and sex ratio

analytic.title: Lessons from the use of non-invasive genetic sampling as a way to estimate Eurasian otter population size and sex ratio

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Given the difficulties in establishing population parameters of elusive animals in the wild by traditional methods, such as trapping, much attention has been given in recent years to non-invasive genetic sampling. Our work compared estimates of population size and sex ratio derived from genetic sampling with the known number and sex of animals released during an otter reintroduction and reports on the pitfalls and opportunities that may be encountered in studies of this kind. This study makes use of 121 samples of otter spraints (faeces) collected over 7 months during a reintroduction in the Upper Thames (UK) where a total of 17 otters was released in two consecutive phases. Spraints were processed with a multiple tubes approach and seven microsatellites were used. Of all collected samples, 19 % were complete for at least five loci, the minimum required for discrimination between individuals. Six out of nine of the otters that were released in the first phase were detected, four males and two females, while none of the otters released in the second phase was detected probably due to a combination of sampling pitfalls and otter behaviour. In particular, the specific sex (mostly females) and dominance composition (lower) of the individuals in the second release group may explain our failure to detect individuals in this group. Taken together, our results add further evidence that genetic sampling approaches represent a potentially accurate and non-invasive route to census populations of otters but that the sampling design should take into account factors like the sex ratio and dominance composition of the population in order to maximise detection and minimise error.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Individual identification via non-invasive genetic sampling is increasingly recognised as very useful for the study of populations of cryptic and endangered species for which estimating population size and monitoring population dynamics play a vital role (e.g. Taberlet et al. 1997;Lucchini et al. 2002). One of the species whose study is most likely to benefit from this approach is the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra), especially those populations living in freshwater habitats where animals tend to be nocturnal and elusive (e.g. Kruuk et al. 1993), whereas those in coastal areas tend to be more diurnal and observable (e.g. Kruuk et al. 1989). Previous approaches to characterise otter populations include surveys for spraints, snow tracking, visual censuses, and radio-tracking, but all four methods have drawbacks (Kruuk et al. 1986(Kruuk et al. , 1993;;Ruiz-Olmo 1995;Hájková et al. 2009). Spraint surveys can provide only a relative index of otter abundance. Snow tracking can only be performed in areas where snow is present for long periods and only in winter. Visual censuses are limited to areas where otters are relatively diurnal. Radio-tracking requires live-trapping and the implantation of transmitters, which are both difficult, have welfare implications and yield limited information on population size. In comparison, non-invasive genetic sampling does not require trapping, manipulation or disturbance of the animals as it is based on the analysis of DNA extracted from otters' spraints (otter faeces) (Dallas and Piertney 1998;Coxon et al. 1999;Dallas et al. 2000;Huang et al. 2005). This approach allows the estimation of many useful parameters, such as population size (Prigioni et al. 2006b), sex ratio (Dallas et al. 2003), and population turnover (Koelewijn et al. 2010); it allows us to derive population trends (Hájková et al. 2007) and offers the opportunity to study dispersal (Janssens et al. 2008) and kinship (Kalz et al. 2006), all of which are important for conservation and management purposes. Moreover it can be used to evaluate the success of reintroduction or translocation projects (Arrendal et al. 2004;Ferrando et al. 2008;Koelewijn et al. 2010). Non-invasive genetic sampling has also been used to provide additional samples to study the genetic structure of otters' populations (e.g. Hájková et al. 2007), although these kind of studies tend mostly to make use of otter tissues obtained from road casualties or museum specimens (e.g. Dallas et al. 1999;Pertoldi et al. 2001;Mucci et al. 2010).

In Europe, the Eurasian otter is currently a species of conservation concern (Ruiz-Olmo et al. 2008) but, in those areas where it enters into conflict with human interests, it is also a species of management concern (Kranz 2000). Being able to estimate with a good degree of accuracy otter's population parameters, such as population size or the sex ratio, in areas where conservation or management of otters is required, is of paramount importance as actions will be based on these estimates. However, there are hurdles to using non-invasive genetic sampling to estimate otter population parameters. Estimates obtained with this method might deviate from the true values of the parameters due to at least three different causes. First, the distribution of otter spraints may not be representative of the true composition of the population as different individuals may be more or less inclined to leave spraints where they can be detected (Kruuk et al. 1986;Kruuk 1992). This can actually result in heterogeneous capture probabilities that can potentially affect the estimation. Second, the choice of the sampling locations and time of sampling may influence estimates (Hájková et al. 2006(Hájková et al. , 2009)). Third, genotyping errors can lead to misidentification of individuals which can lead to either under-or overestimation of population size and of the sex of the individuals (Taberlet et al. 1996;Creel et al. 2003;Hansen et al. 2008). Otter faeces, in particular, yield low quality and quantity of DNA, with overall genotyping success often being low and genotyping errors being at times high (reviewed by Hájková et al. 2009). Therefore sampling this species with non-invasive genetic methods often requires more effort than for other similar species and is more prone to biases (Waits and Leberg 2000) and it is hence important to highlight problems that may arise from the sampling design and learn from studies where the results highlight sampling weaknesses.

Our work presents the results of non-invasive genetic sampling used to detect the minimum number of individuals and the sex ratio of a population of otters by comparing the known number and sex of otters released during a reintroduction with the values of these parameters obtained indirectly through non-invasive genetic sampling. We used a specific sampling strategy throughout the study and we discuss how this may have influenced our success in light of the behaviour of otters.

div.head: Otter release and spraint collection
div.p: This study makes use of spraints collected immediately after an otter reintroduction in 1999 in the Upper Thames (national grid-N 220000, S 187000, E 441000, W 400000). Otters had been virtually extinct from the area for at least 20 years although sporadic signs were found in the 1991-1994 Otter National Survey (Strachan and Jefferies 1996), and the nearest population of wild otters was at about 70 Km on the Avon in the Severn-Trent catchment (Crawford 2003). A survey of 96 sites to confirm that otters were absent from the area was carried out in March 1999 just before the release of the first otters (methods described in Bonesi and Macdonald 2004) (Fig. 1).

Between March and October 1999, a total of 17 otters (6 males and 11 females) was reintroduced by a conservation Non-Governmental Organization, the Otter Trust. This allowed us to (1) obtain high quality DNA profiles of all the otters released from blood samples that were collected prior to the release (typed by Dr. John Dallas at Aberdeen University) and (2) know the maximum number of individuals in the population and their sex ratio. We were thus able to compare the results from the spraint sampling program with the known DNA fingerprints of the released individuals.

The otters were released in two different phases: nine otters were released in groups of two or three at monthly intervals between March and June at one site and then a further eight otters were released in September and October in groups of two or three at two different sites that were 4.5 km from each other and of which the nearest was located approximately 6.5 km from the first site (Fig. 1). Because of the different results, we obtained for these two phases we kept most of the analyses separate. In particular, we consider the first phase of the study to run between March and August 1999 and the second one to run in September and October 1999. Released otters were all less than 2 years old when released and not pregnant (males and females had been kept segregated). In otters, age of first breeding is about 2.5 years, gestation takes 60 to 64 days, and weaning occurs after three months. Under these circumstances, it was unlikely that offspring were present during the course of our study, unless perhaps at the very end. For 1 year after the release, we observed and recorded the expansion of this new population (Fig. 2). For the first 7 months of the study, between April and October 1999, we collected otter spraints to be used for DNA analysis. Spraints were collected on a monthly basis at sites that the otters were known to visit for a total of 7 surveys post-release (c.f.r. Bonesi and Macdonald 2004) (Fig. 2). Apart from the sites surrounding the release sites, sites were selected using intervals between sites of at least 3 km and, where possible, selected so that they coincided with sites surveyed during the National Otter Survey. Each site consisted of a stretch of river 500 m long and overall in the area, we surveyed 96 sites, including the initial survey of early March prior to otter release. We increased the number of sampled sites as the otters expanded their range from the points of release starting with nine sites in late March/April and ending with 51 sites in October (Fig. 2). To make sure that we did not underestimate otter range expansion, we surveyed at least three sites upstream Fig. 1 Location of sites where otter spraints were found between April and October (small black circles). The larger grey circles identify the three areas where otters were released (the area further east was the one used during the first phase of the release; the other two were used during the second phase of the release). The crosses represent the location of otters found dead between October 1999 and December 2000, after the study was concluded. The contour represents the 95 % kernel comprising the area with all the sites surveyed in March 1999 before the otters were released Fig. 2 Location of sampling sites (circles) and 95 % kernels contours used to show incremental areas surveyed in subsequent surveys (number of surveys=8). The first survey, carried out before the otter were released, comprises the largest area (thicker line) and was carried out in March before the otters were released. Kernel contours were calculated in ArcView version 3.2 Home Range module, with the smoothing parameter kept constant at H=5,000. Because of the way we increased the survey area (see "Materials and methods"), the kernel contours can be considered to approximate the area covered by the otters' expansion at each subsequent survey of the last known site where otters had been found during the previous or current survey. Sites were on average 2,185 m apart (SD=1,332, n=50) but around the first release area sites were closer (on average 1,474 m apart SD= 816 m, n=18). Although, more positive sites were found around the first release site than around the second release sites, the effort in searching for these sites was similar in the two areas around the release sites. Before collecting the spraints for DNA fingerprinting, the site was cleaned of all previous spraints and then visited soon after sunrise on one to three consecutive days, and all fresh spraints were collected and stored in 100 % ethanol at -70 °C. Spraints were collected only if deposited the previous night and were always collected before 9:00 a.m.

div.head: DNA laboratory analyses
div.p: The DNA fingerprinting was partly carried out by the authors, partly by a sequencing laboratory at the Department of Zoology in Oxford and partly under commission by two specialised laboratories (Tepnel Life Sciences PLC, Manchester and the Department of Haematology at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh).

DNA was extracted from otter spraints using the CTAB/ GITC/diatom/VectaSpin method (Parsons et al. 1999). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis, with an otter specific primer set (L. lutra mitochondrial DNA for cytochrome B; Table 1), was used to determine the suitability of each extracted DNA sample for profiling (Jansman et al. 2001). PCR products were analysed on a 2 % agarose gel and samples producing a single band at approximately the 504 base pair position were deemed suitable for DNA genotyping. PCR analysis was repeated on those samples that failed the initial analysis. Samples failing both PCR analyses were not progressed.

Seven tetranucleotide microsatellite loci were used to genotype each sample (Table 1). The PCR primers and conditions for the first six loci, originally published by Dallas and Piertney (1998), were re-designed to allow the simultaneous analysis of multiple loci within the sample, separated on the basis of size and fluorescent label (Table 1). The re-designed primers enabled the simultaneous analysis of seven microsatellites within two lanes of an electrophoresis gel using two fluorescent labels (TETgreen and FAM-blue). The seven loci were amplified in two multiplex reactions (here called primer sets A and C). Primer set A amplified loci Lut-715, Lut-717, Lut-782, and Lut-902. Primer set C amplified loci Lut-701, Lut-832, and Lut-833. Both primer sets were amplified in 15 μl reactions as follows: 1× Taq buffer (AmpliTaq Gold PCR buffer II), 2.0 mM MgCl 2 , 0.25 mM each dNTP, 1.0 μl primer mix, 4.0 Units of Taq (AmpliTaq Gold, Applied Biosystems), and 1.0 μl template DNA for blood samples, and 5.0 μl template DNA for spraint samples.

Samples were amplified with a modified temperature cycling system known as sub-cycling PCR (Liu and Sommer 1998). With this method, the annealing and extension steps are sub-cycled within each full denaturing/annealing/extension cycle. The reaction cycle required an initial denaturation of 95 °C for 12 min, followed by 15 full PCR cycles of 94 °C for 15 s, 54 °C for 5 s, and 65 °C for 10 s, with five sub-cycles of the annealing (54 °C) and extension (65 °C) temperatures within each full cycle; followed by another 20 full cycles of 94 °C for 10 s, 54 °C for 10 s, and 65 °C for 15 s, with five sub-cycles of the annealing and extension temperatures within each full cycle; then a final extension of 65 °C for 30 min. PCR products were visualised on 6 % polyacrylamide/ urea gels on an ABI 377 automated sequencer (Applied Biosystems). DNA sizing was determined by the inclusion of an internal standard (Genescan-500 TAMRA, Perkin Elmer). Data were extracted from lanes and sizes with Genescan software and the alleles were sized with Genotyper software. Allele binning was based on the results of the blood analyses. Allele values for binning were chosen as a list of integer numbers with a step of four base pairs.

div.head: DNA data analyses
div.p: To estimate the number of loci necessary to distinguish between individuals with certainty, we computed the probability of identity amongst siblings (P IDsib ), because otters that were related to each other were present in our sample (Waits et al. 2001). The P IDsib of all loci, is the upper limit of the possible ranges of the probability of identity (P ID ) in a population and thus provides the most conservative number of loci required to resolve all otters, including relatives. An overall P IDsib , of less than 0.05 giving a 95 % confidence was considered sufficient to discriminate between individuals for the purpose of population estimation (Mills et al. 2000). We calculated P IDsib using a data set of genotypes obtained from the blood DNA of the released otters. The number of loci necessary to distinguish between individuals was estimated with the program GenAlEx 6.1 (Peakall and Smouse 2006).

To avoid incorrect genotypes due to allelic dropout, false alleles or sporadic contamination, we used the multiple tubes approach suggested by Taberlet et al. (1996), with up to seven PCR replicates for the same sample. We retained the rule that an allele was accepted only if it was observed at least twice, therefore accepting loci that gave rise to the same heterozygous genotype twice. In our study, following Frantz et al. (2003), a homozygote was accepted after three positive PCRs gave rise to the same, single allele; otherwise, we considered the locus to have potentially been heterozygous with only one allele detected and one allele missing. We then constructed consensus multilocus genotypes, i.e. the most likely genotype based on all PCR amplifications of a sample, following the rules described above.

Faecal DNA extracts are generally of low quantity and quality and when pipetting diluted and degraded DNA, stochastic pipetting errors, PCR primers annealing in nontarget sites (PCR jumping), and sporadic contamination may lead to PCR-artefacts (Gerloff et al. 1995;Taberlet et al. 1997). In evaluating markers, we considered that there could be two kinds of error, allelic dropout (false negatives), when only one of the alleles at a heterozygous locus is evident; and false allele detection (false positives) when one or both alleles for a given locus provide a result that does not correspond to the true alleles for that sample. Frequency of allelic dropout and false alleles were computed separately as the number of errors detected, divided by the total number of cases in which an error can be detected using the consensus genotypes as a baseline (Broquet and Petit 2004). Error rates were computed with the software GIMLET 1.3.3 and only for those samples that yielded at least five positive loci (c.f.r. Arrendal et al. 2007). In the case of allelic dropout only heterozygous loci were considered and the errors were calculated for each locus across all samples and for each sample across all loci. We also tested for evidence of null alleles in our 17 samples derived from the otters' blood using the software MicroChecker (http://www.microchecker.hull.ac.uk) using a 95 % confidence interval (Van Oosterhout et al. 2004).

div.head: Population size and sex ratio estimation
div.p: In order to assess how well the non-invasive genetic approach was at determining the minimum number of otters released, we compared consensus genotypes obtained from spraint samples with the reference genotypes obtained from the blood samples of the released otters. To do so we used the module 'Identify several genotypes' in the program GIMLET 1.3.3. (Valière 2002). Incomplete genotypes were considered only if at least five loci were amplified successfully (i.e. the minimum number of loci necessary to discriminate between individuals as indicated by probability of identity analysis). Although these incomplete genotypes might have belonged to a new individual, we assigned them to complete ones to ensure our population estimates were conservative.

We assessed the minimum number of animals present by counting the number of unique genotypes recorded among all spraint samples collected at the study site and restricted the sampling to between one and seven months after release in order to minimise the chance of dispersal movements and of reproduction. We also estimated population size with the capture-mark-recapture-based program CAPWIRE developed specifically for non-invasive genetic sampling (Miller et al. 2005) and particularly suitable for small populations with high heterogeneity of capture (Luikart et al. 2010). This software is designed to take into account data with multiple observations of an individual. The likelihood ratio test with p<0.1 was used to choose between the even capture probability model and the two innate rates model (TRIM) that considers that there are two types of individuals, one that is harder and one that is easier to capture. Population size was estimated separately for the first phase of the release, taking into account the samples collected until August, and then for the first and second phases combined, taking into account the samples collected until the end of the study. CAPWIRE assumes that the population is closed and this assumption was more likely to be satisfied in the first phase of the release, than in the second phase during which it is possible, although unlikely, that reproduction occurred.

We also determined the sex ratio of the population based on non-invasive genetic sampling and compared it with the known sex ratio of the released population. As otters were being released while spraint samples were collected, the sex ratio in the population was corrected for the number of days that otters of a given sex had been present, i.e. the sex ratio was calculated by dividing the number of days males were present by the number of days females were present in each release phase. We did not use a specific genetic marker for sex determination but, as we knew the sex of each individual otter, we used the spraint DNA profile to attribute an otter to a given individual and hence to a given sex.

div.head: Results
div.p: Probability of identity, genotyping results, and error rates P IDsib , calculated from the reference genotypes of all the 17 released otters, predicted that at least five loci were necessary to distinguish with 95 % certainty between the different individuals (P IDsib for five loci=0.029, P IDsib for seven loci= 0.005). The five most informative loci were Lut-782, Lut-902, Lut-832, Lut-833, and Lut-701. Heterozygosity ranged between 0.04 and 0.87 (Table 2). P IDsib , calculated from the reference genotypes of the nine otters released up to June 1999, also predicted that at least five loci were necessary to distinguish with 95 % certainty between the different individuals (P IDsib for five loci=0.050; P IDsib for seven loci=0.013).

A total of 121 spraint samples were collected, of these 89 were collected between April and August, during and after the release of the first nine otters, while 32 were collected in September and October when the remaining 8 otters were released at a different site. DNA was successfully extracted from all samples, of which 105 samples passed the mtDNA cytochrome b amplification, and of these 85 (70 %) were progressed to the profiling stage (genotyped). All 85 samples underwent at least four PCRs with primer set A and four PCRs with primer set C; 51 samples underwent one additional PCR with primer set C and 34 underwent one additional PCR with primer set C and three additional PCRs with primer set A, taking the total amount of PCRs to five and seven for these samples respectively. A total of 23 samples produced genotypes that were complete for at least 5 loci (19 % of all collected samples); the remaining 62 samples had fewer than 5 loci. We recalculated P IDsib excluding the locus or couple of loci which failed and found that P IDsib for the remaining six or five loci was always below the chosen threshold of 5 %.

A total of 11 blood samples from the released otters were also re-typed within the context of this study (while all 17 blood samples were typed by J.Dallas) in order to perform detailed analyses on PCR success. Of these samples three belonged to otters released prior to June and eight belonged to otters released in September and October. The proportion of positive PCRs was much higher for blood samples (mean across loci=0.77, SD=0.07, n=11) than for spraint samples (mean across loci=0.42, SD=0.12, n=85) indicating that DNA extracted from blood was typed more successfully than that extracted from spraints. If only the 23 spraint samples (17 from the first phase and 6 from the second phase) that yielded at least five successful loci were considered, then the percentage of positive PCRs was higher than when considering all 85 spraint samples (mean across loci= 0.66, SD=0.11, n=23) but still lower than when considering blood samples. The percentage of positive PCRs for each locus is shown in Table 2.

The mean frequency of allelic dropout for the 23 samples that presented more than five loci was 15.4 % among loci (SD = 0.010) and 20.4 % among samples (SD = 0.172). Studies have shown that longer PCR products tend to correspond to lower PCR success rate and higher frequency of allelic dropout especially when DNA is of low quality and quantity (Buchan et al. 2005;Broquet et al. 2007). Even though the original primers by Dallas and Piertney (1998) were redesigned for this study, and this has lead to an increase of PCR product size for some markers (Table 1), allele length did not seem to affect the proportion of allelic dropout (Spearman's rho=-0.48, p=0.851 one tail, n=6 loci excluding Lut-715 that was highly homozygous) or the proportion of positive PCRs (Spearman's rho=-0.32, p= 0.239 one tail, n=7 loci). False alleles were recorded with a frequency of 2.7 % (SD=0.021) among loci and of 2.9 % (SD = 0.032) among samples. The proportion of allelic dropout and false allele rates for each locus is shown in Table 2. Null alleles were not present in our samples.

div.head: Number of otters and sex ratio
div.p: If one considers all the 17 genotypes with more than five positive loci from samples collected up until August 1999, then six out of nine of the released otters were detected when these were compared with the reference genotypes derived from blood samples (Fig. 3), and all the assignments were consistent with the date of release of the otters.

There was considerable capture heterogeneity among individuals, with a few individuals being represented by a disproportionate number of spraints. A total of seven spraints belonged to a single individual whose profile corresponded to otter 9♂, five spraints belonged to another one whose profile corresponded to otter 10♀, two spraints corresponded to the profile of otter 7♂, and one spraint each matched the profiles of otter 8♂ and otter 14♂. In order to match the remaining genotype, sample 74, with one of the released otters, one had to accept that an error had occurred and a false allele had appeared. Sample 74 was closest to the profile of otter 6♀. If we were to accept only genotypes that were complete for all 7 loci then we would have detected only four otters; if we were to accept genotypes that were complete for the six most informative loci (all but excluding Lut-701) then five otters would have been detected. The three otters that were not detected with non-invasive genetic sampling in the first phase of the release were otter 15♂ released in May, and otters 22♀ and 23♀ released in June. These, together with otter 14♂, were the last four otters to be released before the program re-started in September with the release of a further eight otters.

The six samples that produced genotypes with five or more loci and that were collected in the second phase of the release (September-October 1999), all belonged to otters released up to June 1999 (four belonged to otter 7♂, one to otter 9♂, and one to otter 6♀). No spraints from the eight otters (seven females and one male) that were released in September and October were detected with non-invasive genetic sampling.

For the first phase of the release and for the first and second phases combined, CAPWIRE analyses were based on the TRIM model as this was indicated by the likelihood ratio test in both cases as the most appropriate for the data. When using a 95 % confidence interval for the first phase of the release, the CAPWIRE point estimate of population size was 8 individuals (range, 6-9), while for both phases combined it was seven individuals (range, 6-9). In the first phase, two individuals were classified as "easier to capture" while six as "harder to capture"; while for both phases, combined these values were three and four, respectively. The average number of observations (samples) per individual was 2.8 for the first phase and 3.8 for both phases combined.

The sample size was small, but there seemed to be a tendency for otters that were released earlier to present more spraints in the sample compared with otters that were released later. Of the 23 spraints that yield a successful genotype, 13 spraints were from the two otters released in March, 9 spraints were from the three otters released in April, and one spraint was from the two otters released in May and none belonged to any of the ten individuals released from June onward.

The overall sex ratio when taking into account the number of days in which males and females were present, was of 1.02 males/1 female (952 male days and 929 female days), while if simply counting the individuals of each sex the ratio was 0.55 m:1f (6 males and 11 females). Non-invasive genetic sampling produced an estimate of the sex ratio that was strongly skewed toward males. When counting the individuals of each sex identified with this method, the sex ratio was 2.00 males/1 female (four males and two females). When counting the number of spraints of each sex the estimate was even more biased at 2.29 males/1 female (16 male spraints and 7 female spraints). However, due to the small sample size, when comparing the number of otters of each sex released and identified no significant difference was found (Fisher's exact test p=0.19), while when comparing the number of otters of each sex released with the number of spraints of each sex identified non-invasively a significant difference was found (Fisher's exact test p= 0.03). The inclusion of a higher density of sampled sites around the first release site than around the second release sites (due to the fact that we found many more positive sites in that area) may have further biased our results toward Fig. 3 Cumulative number of released otters and estimate of the number of otters as derived from non-invasive genetic sampling males given that they were present in a higher proportion in the animals released at the first site.

div.head: Evaluation of the non-invasive genetic method
div.p: In our study, only 19 % of the samples collected yielded genotypes adequate to identify single individuals according to the P IDsib statistics. This figure, albeit low, is within the range reported by other authors in similar studies of L. lutra, where success rates varied between 14 and 73 % (Jansman et al. 2001;Dallas et al. 2003;Hung et al. 2004;Prigioni et al. 2006aPrigioni et al. , 2006b;;Kalz et al. 2006;Arrendal et al. 2007;Ferrando et al. 2008;Janssens et al. 2008;Lanszki et al. 2008;Hájková et al. 2009;Koelewijn et al. 2010). Our relatively low success in obtaining genotypes could have been due to several factors. First, our samples were collected between April and October, when air temperature is relatively high. Amplification success of spraint DNA has been found to be significantly affected by temperature (Hájková et al. 2006;Janssens 2006), and, therefore, sampling at low temperatures may have increased our success rate. Second, in our study, spraints were stored for 2 years before the DNA was extracted. Lampa et al. (2008;but see Hájková et al. 2006) found that the highest amplification success is obtained when samples are extracted immediately after collection and a 2-year delay could have been partly responsible for the degradation of the DNA. Third, we collected spraints in a way that did not maximise our chances to obtain gut cells that held the DNA. In the field, we collected the whole spraint, placed it in a tube with 100 % ethanol, and then shook the tube so that the ethanol permeated the sample as much as possible. This protocol reduced considerably our chances to pick up the sloughed gut cells found in the external layer of the spraint. A pilot study by Lampa et al. (2008) showed that a swipe with a cotton swab of the external layer of the spraint is a better method for collecting the sample. Fourth, only 17 of the 121 samples (14 %) we collected were made only of anal jelly. Several authors found that samples consisting only of jelly tend to yield a very high PCR success rate (Coxon et al. 1999;Hájková et al. 2006;Lampa et al. 2008). Indeed samples of anal jelly were in higher proportion in the sample of successfully typed spraints (5 out of 23 or 22 %) than in our original sample, but still only 5 of the 17 anal jelly samples were successfully typed.

The frequencies of allelic dropout and false alleles of the 23 samples that presented more than five loci were within the values found in other otters studies (Arrendal et al. 2007;Ferrando et al. 2008;Hájková et al. 2009;Koelewijn et al. 2010). To limit bias due to errors and increase the reliability of the identification, one would ideally carry out further PCRs with the multiple-tubes procedure proposed by Taberlet et al. (1996). However, in our case this further analysis was impractical due to the paucity of the DNA extract, a common problem when working with otter faecal DNA (Coxon et al. 1999;Hájková et al. 2006;Lampa et al. 2008). This problem could have been circumvented if more samples had been found, so that we could have had at least five samples per otter. However, at least in our population, a few individuals left a disproportionate number of spraints. It is possible that an increased field effort in the second phase may have yielded sufficient samples to identify the individuals whose signs were less abundant, but our survey in its second phase was limited by the difficulty of finding suitable sites to provide sufficient numbers of spraints.

These problems, coupled with the low success rates of DNA extraction and typing that characterises otter spraints (Lampa et al. 2008), resulted in a relatively low rate of amplification success. However, albeit low, this rate allowed identifying a relatively high proportion of the otters released in the first phase but not those released in the second phase.

div.head: Comparison of genetic estimates with composition of released group
div.p: We obtained very different results in terms of the ability to census otters with non-invasive genetic sampling when considering the first and the second phase of the release and this was, at least in part, due to the fact that the sample size for the second phase was much smaller. Overall, with the genetic sampling we detected six out of nine of the otters released in the first phase between March and August 1999, underestimating the minimum number of individuals present in this phase by about 30 %. In a similar study, where 30 otters were released and monitored through noninvasive genetic sampling, the authors were able to detect 50 % of the released animals (Koelewijn et al. 2010). The three otters that we were not able to detect by this methodology were otter 15♂, otter 22♀, and otter 23♀. Otters 23♀ and 15♂ were known to be alive and were probably in the area on the grounds that they were found dead within 6 km of the release point after the study had been concluded (Fig. 1). In contrast, otter 22♀ was never detected and so may have left the area or died during the study, making it plausible that the true number of otters in the population was actually eight and not nine.

With the CAPWIRE software, estimates between 2.5 and 3.0 observations per individual should be sufficient to obtain a precise estimate of population size (Miller et al. 2005). In our case, an average of 3.8 observations per individual if considering both the first and second release phases, or 2.8 observations if we consider the first phase of the release only, were made. If, for the first phase, we take the upper limit of the confidence interval obtained with CAPWIRE of nine otters, this actually correctly identified the number of otters released in the first phase. However, the assumptions of the CAPWIRE model were not fully satisfied by the characteristics of our population and hence the results must be taken with care. Indeed, although we can assume that for the duration of the study the population was closed as no immigration was likely to occur, the otters were released in a staggered manner effectively rendering the population open. Moreover, our sampling area was increased throughout the study to take into account the expanding population thereby affecting our sampling intensity. In particular, these violations of the assumptions are likely to reduce the reliability of the estimate of the number of individuals that are easy or difficult to capture. While for the first phase of the release we were able to detect a relatively high proportion of the released otters and the estimates obtained are realistic, we were unable to detect any of the otters released in the second phase.

The difference in the number of samples that we were able to collect in the first and the second phase of the release may be due to several reasons. First, we collected spraint samples for a much shorter time after the second group of eight otters was released in September and October; indeed we stopped collecting spraints for DNA analyses at the end of October, while the last three otters were released just a few weeks earlier at the beginning of October. Spraints of the first group of nine otters were collected for at least five months after the last two otters were released. Second, we found it more difficult to find sprainting sites around the two areas where otters were released in the second phase. Our inability to find these sites was unlikely to be due to the topology of the area, as all three release areas were relatively close and habitat did not differ substantially.

One of the reasons why we were unable to find sprainting sites around the second release area may be due to dominance factors between individual otters. If marking with spraints reflects the social status of the individual, as suggested for males of the river otter Lontra canadensis (Rostain et al. 2004), it is possible that otters released later in the first phase or those released in the second phase, found themselves in an area already occupied by other otters, and hence tended to mark less. It is also possible that some of these otters quickly dispersed out of the survey area. We know that at least five of the 11 undetected otters were still probably in the area during the study having been found dead in the area later within a radius of 3 to 15 km from their release site (Fig. 1). However, the six remaining otters may have moved out of the area so quickly that we were unable to detect them. It is known that otters that are first released tend to occupy the most suitable sites for feeding while those released later tend to disperse further (Sjöåsen 1997;Saavedra 2002). However, given that at least five otters were likely to be still in the area, our data seem to suggest that there is also the possibility that otters released later may have marked less, possibly because they were of lower status compared with the ones released earlier.

Another possible reason why we were unable to find sprainting sites around the second release area was that the second phase group was composed mostly of females; indeed seven out of the eight animals released in this group were females. In this study, even for the first group, estimates based on non-invasive genetic sampling tended to be strongly biased toward males; indeed males were identified proportionally more than females and they tended to leave more spraints than females. This observation raises the possibility that non-invasive genetic sampling may provide a biased estimate of the true sex ratio of the population. For this method to be useful in the estimation of otter population parameters, ideally at least two assumptions need to be satisfied: (1) that the spraints that are successfully genotyped are representative of all the spraints collected and (2) that otter defecation rates and detectability of spraints are equal among sexes and age classes and are independent of social status (Kohn et al. 1999). In our case, we collected 100 % of the spraints that we found after clearing the site, but of those only 19 % yielded genotypes. The low genotyping success rate could have lead to a bias in the estimate of the sex ratio if, by chance, more male spraints ended up in the sub-sample of successfully genotyped spraints. There are, however, studies that reach a much higher percentage of genotyping success and they still report a male bias (Table 3). If we exclude the study by Hung et al. (2004) that may have overestimated the population (Hájková et al. 2009) and the study by Koelewijn et al. (2010) that detected 2010) report only the sex ratio of offspring a These studies reported respectively ten and two additional individuals of unknown sex and the value of the sex ratio may be affected by them mostly new born individuals, then most of the other studies, namely seven out of eight, found a male sex bias when estimating this parameter with non-invasive genetic sampling (Table 3). The possibility that females are more likely to go undetected with this method is also supported by the fact that both our study and that of Koelewijn et al. (2010) found that male otters tended to leave a higher number of spraints, thereby seemingly increasing the chance to detect males over females when using spraints collected on land (otters can also defecate in the water (Kruuk 2006)). Kruuk (1992), using behavioural observations of otters, found that defecation rates of males and females in coastal Scotland varied according to season with males tending to defecate more than females on land between May and August, but not at other times of the year (Kruuk 1992, Fig. 1a).

Unfortunately, there are no observational studies of otter defecation rates where sex can be distinguished in freshwater areas and in areas where reproduction is not strongly seasonal, although seasonality in sprainting activity has been reported in areas with these characteristics (Macdonald and Mason 1987;Kruuk 2006;Georgiev 2008).

There are other methods used to estimate the sex ratio of otter populations that yield an estimate biased towards males. Dallas et al. (2003) compared estimates of sex ratio derived from spraints collected over 14 months with estimates derived from carcasses, mostly of road-kills, found in the same area over 11 years and found that the two methods yielded comparable estimates. With both methods males were found to be more abundant than females (sex ratio spraint samples=1.48 m:1f; sex ratio road kills=1.41 males/ 1 female) and indeed most studies based on road kills tend to find more males than females (e.g. Ruiz-Olmo et al. 1998;Philcox et al. 1999;Dallas et al. 2003;Koelewijn et al. 2010). Rather than representing a bias in the true sex ratio of the population, the higher proportion of males in road kill samples seems to be due to the fact that many more young males than females tend to be killed on roads because of their dispersal behaviour (Koelewijn et al. 2010). Therefore, both methods, non-invasive genetic sampling and otter road kill sampling, potentially provide a biased estimate of the true sex ratio of the population.

If in freshwater habitats where all non-invasive genetic studies of Eurasian otters have been conducted, males do actually spraint more often on dry land than do females, at least at certain times of year, there is the possibility that in these habitats otters use spraints for reasons other than signalling the use of resources as hypothesised by Kruuk for coastal otters (Kruuk 1992(Kruuk , 2006)). In particular, Koelewijn et al. (2010) found that dominant males with large territories were represented more frequently in their spraint sample raising the possibility that Eurasian otters, like river otters, may use spraints to signal status (Rostain et al. 2004), and possibly also territorial defence and/or reproduction. This would also explain why in one study of non-invasive genetic sampling where age was known, younger individuals that were more likely to be in a lowdominance and non-reproductive status showed a sex ratio that was close to one (Koelewijn et al. 2010).

A male bias in the ability to detect otters with noninvasive genetic sampling and possibly a dominance issue, coupled with our low success rate, and with the short time that we collected the spraints after the second phase are the likely causes of our failure to detect the second group of released otters.

div.head: Conclusions and lessons learned
div.p: Establishing protocols for genetic sampling necessitates independent validation of parameter estimates, but alternative methods of estimating population parameters of otters such as snow tracking (Arrendal et al. 2007;Hájková et al. 2009) or road kills (Dallas et al. 2003) do have limitations themselves and are also prone to biases as discussed above. Our study took advantage of a controlled release of otters as an independent way to estimate population parameters to compare with genetic sampling. Our study had its own limitations, due mostly to the small number of released otters, the small number of spraints that provided genotypes, the temporal limits of the study, and the fact that we studied animals that had just been released rather than an established population. Even under these circumstances, we learned that we could have improved the success of our study if (1) we collected samples in a way that better preserved the gut cells from which DNA is extracted; (2) we extracted the DNA immediately;

(3) we tried to extract greater quantities of DNA; and (4) we adapted our sampling strategy to increase the number of samples collected around the second release area, possibly by increasing the frequency of sampling as well as the number of sample sites. However, in spite of these limitations our study has highlighted, amongst other things, that non-invasive genetic sampling may provide biased estimates of the sex composition of otter populations, and that status may affect spraint deposition and hence detection. To be able to interpret the results of noninvasive genetic studies in the Eurasian otter and adjust the estimates obtained it seems therefore important to better understand the effect of sex, status, and reproduction on sprainting activity. Experimental studies where the sex, reproductive status and dominance of the individual that is inspecting the spraint and that of the individual that has deposited the spraint can be identified, like those carried out for the river otter (Rostain et al. 2004) and other species (Jordan et al. 2011), may contribute to understanding the function of sprainting in the Eurasian otter and hence provide a key to better interpret the results of non-invasive genetic estimates of population parameters.
